data.content_ref: inline:The target misidentifies the dominant single mechanism. The problem context asks for the single mechanism that best explains why the nighttime UHI gap is larger in some cities than in others. The target's mechanism is aerodynamic roughness/wind-shielding, and it asserts the cross-city variance scales with building density because taller, denser buildings increase friction and suppress cooling. But the cross-city variance of nocturnal UHI is most strongly controlled by the sky view factor (radiative geometry), not by roughness. On the clear, calm nights specified by the problem, wind is already weak, so additional roughness-driven wind suppression is a second-order effect. The first-order reason denser/built-up cities cool more slowly is that narrow street canyons reduce the view of the cold sky, trapping longwave radiation and slowing radiative cooling. The target omits sky view factor entirely and instead makes building density matter only through wind friction, which is a weaker and less direct explanation for the clear, calm night condition. This is a substantive error against the problem as stated.
